title: Choosing SLIs by service type
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A good indicator is a ratio of good events to valid events, correlates with user happiness, and can be measured reliably.
For a request service use availability, the share of valid requests that succeed, and latency, the share served faster than a threshold.
For a data pipeline use freshness, the share of time that data is newer than a limit, and correctness, the share of records that pass checks.
Server side metrics are easy but miss failures before the request arrives.
Define which events are valid and which are good in words first.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: Green dashboards and angry customers
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
The availability dashboard showed one hundred percent while customers could not check out.
An operator runs a command such as: curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}\n" https://shop.example.com/checkout
The indicator counted only the share of responses that were not server errors, and the checkout page returned 200 after eleven seconds, so it counted as good.
Customers abandoned the page. This keeps the next step safe and easy to check.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Using CPU or memory as an SLI.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Running an SLO workshop and writing an error budget policy
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Include the product owner who knows what matters to users, engineers who know how the service fails, the on call lead and a stakeholder who can accept trade offs.
List the critical user journeys.
Start from what users need and what the service has achieved, and not from a round number.
Write down what happens when the budget is spent.
Review SLOs every quarter. This keeps the next step safe and easy to check.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The SLO that nobody could use
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A team met its SLO every month, but release pressure continued and reliability work never got time.
An operator runs a command such as: cat slo-policy.md | head -3
The SLO existed but the policy had never been approved, so a low budget changed nothing.
When a major incident used most of the budget, the next release went ahead anyway.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: No product owner in the workshop.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Alert quality and on call health
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: For each alert count how often it fired, how often it needed action, how long it took to resolve and when it fired.
A page means a human must act now to protect users.
Page on symptoms users feel, such as error budget burn, and keep cause alerts as supporting information for diagnosis.
Set a target such as at most two actionable pages per shift and track against it.
Write a short handover note with open issues, recent changes and risky times.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: Three pages a night for a month
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A small team lost two engineers after a month of frequent night pages.
An operator runs a command such as: cat pages-last-30-days.csv | awk -F, 'NR>1 {c[$2]++} END {for (k in c) print c[k], k}' | sort -rn | head -3
The three noisiest alerts were cause based and needed no action most of the time.
The team moved the disk and CPU alerts to tickets with trend based predictions, replaced the restart alert with a burn rate page and set a target of two actionable pages per shift.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Paging on causes that need no action.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Tabletops and game days: how to facilitate
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A tabletop is a discussion of a scenario with no systems touched, and it tests decisions, roles and communication.
Pick a realistic and specific failure, such as the primary database loses its leader during a sale.
The facilitator runs the clock and gives injects.
Agree the scope, the systems that may be touched and an abort word that anyone can use.
Hold a short review straight after, then write findings as actions with an owner and a date, such as update the runbook, add an alert or practise the failover again.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The runbook that pointed to a deleted server
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A game day showed that the failover step named a host that no longer existed.
An operator runs a command such as: grep -n "failover" runbooks/db-primary.md | head -2
The scribe recorded that responders lost eight minutes before they found the current procedure.
The facilitator did not rescue them.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: A facilitator who solves the problem for the team.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Testing resilience in pipelines: load, soak and fault injection
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A load test shows how the service behaves at expected and peak traffic.
Use traffic that resembles production in mix and shape, not a single endpoint at constant rate.
Run the service at steady load for a long time and watch memory, file descriptors, connection counts and latency over time.
Add delay or errors to a dependency call, stop a replica, or block a network path, and check that timeouts, retries, circuit breakers and fallbacks do what the design says.
Use the SLO signals as gates: a canary release receives a small share of traffic, and the pipeline compares its error rate and latency with the baseline.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The leak that only showed on day three
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A service that passed every test ran out of file descriptors three days after release.
An operator runs a command such as: ls /proc/$(pgrep -o app)/fd | wc -l
The tests ran for ten minutes and the leak of one descriptor per slow request needed days to show.
A soak test of twelve hours at steady load, which the team added to the nightly pipeline, found the same growth within hours on the next release candidate.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Load tests with unrealistic traffic.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: The reliability programme: reviews, roadmaps and reporting
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Before a service takes real traffic, review it against a checklist: SLOs and alerts exist, runbooks are written, capacity and failure behaviour have been tested, backups restore, ownership is clear and dependencies are known.
Keep a list of known risks with likelihood, impact and an owner.
Turn the highest risks into planned work with estimates and put it on the same roadmap as features.
Give leaders one page each month: SLO status and budget for the main services, the biggest open risks, the incidents with their impact and the progress of the roadmap.
Track mean time to detect and to recover, the number of customer visible incidents, repeat incidents and pages per shift.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The same outage three times in a year
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A certificate based outage recurred because the follow up work was never scheduled.
An operator runs a command such as: grep -c "status: open" postmortem-actions.csv
Twenty seven actions from earlier reviews were still open and only four were done, because they had no owners and no place on the roadmap.
After the third outage, leadership asked for a reliability programme.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Readiness reviews as a rubber stamp.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.
